Remove the close C6 splitter: its saleable tops are worth slightly less than its annual cost and its bottoms remain unsold, so bypassing it should improve net profit.

Restore the best plant and trim the expensive octane/nonane splitter. The wide boiling-point gap should allow much less rectification, boil-up, and pressure drop while retaining both saleable products.

Recover the currently discarded hexane/naphthene stream with a dedicated polishing split. It contains roughly $249M/yr of saleable blend value, enough to justify a modest additional column if both cuts reach 95%.

Continue the successful small trim on the octane/nonane splitter. Both premium products still have purity margin, so a modest further duty reduction may improve profit.
Continue the profitable small duty trim on the octane/nonane splitter. Both premium products still have margin, so a further modest reduction should lower cost with little revenue loss.

Continue the profitable octane/nonane duty trim. Both premium products retain purity margin, so another small reduction should lower annual cost with little revenue loss.

Restore the best plant and make conservative duty trims on the C6 splitter and terminal octane/nonane column. Both have saleable-product purity margin, and these changes avoid the convergence-sensitive light-end columns.
Restore the best design and test one conservative trim of the C6 front-end splitter. Its main blend product has ample purity margin, and the previous similar trim was profitable.
Continue the two profitable conservative duty trims: the heavy terminal products retain premium-grade margin, and the C6 blend has ample purity margin.

Return to the best four-column design and add only the small C4/C5 splitter. A higher boil-up should carry most N-butane overhead while rejecting isopentane bottoms, potentially qualifying one large C4 blend instead of two unsaleable cuts.

Increase the feed-column boil-up to recover the roughly 300 mol/s of C5 currently lost into the heavy bottoms, while keeping the downstream light-end settings fixed to measure the purity and cost trade-off.
Restore the best five-column design and add one small propane/C4 splitter on the discarded 207 mol/s stream. Both outlets should qualify as blends, adding revenue for limited extra cost.

Sharpen only the final octane/nonane splitter in the current heavy-end train. Its 65/34 feed is already well positioned, so this directly tests whether the large octane and nonane revenues can be unlocked without changing the profitable light end.

Restore the best plant and test whether the profitable heptane/octane splitter can lose ten stages without dropping either product below its sale threshold.

Recover the currently unsold 91%-heptane stream with a dedicated polishing split. Removing the lighter C6 naphthenes overhead should unlock heptane sales without sacrificing the profitable octane bottoms.

Sharpen the cyclohexane/heptane polish split. The current overhead still carries about 110 mol/s of unsold heptane, so a sharper cut should recover most of that value while retaining the 98% heptane bottoms.

Recover the two discarded intermediate cuts with small polishers: cyclohexane/heptane is an easy split, and the octane/nonane overhead can yield two additional pure products rather than being discarded.

Restore the best plant and slightly increase boil-up in the octane/nonane pre-split. The octane overhead is 98.25% pure, so sending a little more octane overhead could dilute its heptane impurity enough to earn the 99% premium.
Continue the measured improvement in the octane/nonane pre-split. A small further boil-up increase should dilute the heptane impurity in the octane overhead while retaining nonane recovery.
